asSun.p: Scorpio is Death's sign, which is why the card comes to you with a Scorpio Sun, the same way The Emperor goes to an Aries and Strength goes to a Leo. Scorpio is fixed water, and its old ruler is Mars, with Pluto added by modern astrologers. The Sun itself has no special standing in Scorpio. It isn't strengthened there and it isn't weakened either. It's a visitor in somebody else's house, and it picks up the manners of the host. So your sense of who you are has Mars in it, the fighter, only the fighting mostly happens out of sight. Fixed water doesn't rush about. It sits deep and cold and still on top, and it's very hard to drain. Have a look at the rider on the card for a second. It isn't galloping. The horse is walking, and everyone in front of it has to decide what they're going to do about that.

You decide things once. It can take you a long time to get there, and the people around you often don't see the deciding happen, but when you're done you're done, and the old job or the old friend or the old way of doing Christmas just stops existing for you. Your mate spends six months complaining about a flatmate and you say, fairly flatly, 'so move'. At work there's a restructure coming and you've quietly updated your CV a fortnight before the announcement, because you'd read the room months earlier. Someone at a barbecue asks what you do, and you give them the short version and then ask them something back that's slightly too personal, and they tell you. You're private about what you want, too. You tell people after you've got it, sometimes years after.

The less obvious gift is that you let people change. Because you've shed a few versions of yourself, you don't hold anyone to who they were at nineteen. A friend who got sober, a sister who used to be awful to you, a colleague who messed up badly last year, you'll deal with the person standing in front of you. That's rarer than it sounds. There's also a very practical side to it. When someone dies, or a business folds, or a marriage ends, you're the one who can make the phone calls, find the paperwork, cancel the direct debits and tell the kids in plain words. Other people freeze at the admin of an ending. You get on with it, and it's a real kindness, even if from outside it looks a bit cold.

Most people know a Scorpio Sun can burn a bridge. What they notice less is how much you keep back as insurance. You tend to know more about everyone's situation than they know about yours, and part of you likes it that way. It feels safe. You'll have an exit plan in a relationship that's going perfectly well, a savings account nobody else knows about, a version of events you haven't told your business partner yet. Mars rules the sign, and a Mars that can't fight in the open fights by holding cards. The cost is that the people close to you feel slightly audited. Your partner tells you some small thing they got wrong, and they can see you file it. You don't have to show every card. Show a few more to the people who've earned it, before they give up asking.

When something goes badly wrong, the first thing a Scorpio Sun does is go very calm and very quiet. Lose a job and you've told nobody by dinner time. Lose a parent and you run the funeral with a steady face. Underneath, you've already started working out who knew what and when, because part of you treats every blow as information. A week later the Mars side turns up. You cut someone off, often the wrong someone, or you throw yourself at the gym or a spreadsheet at eleven at night. The people around you get a closed door and a polite voice, and they can't tell whether they're being blamed. What helps is telling one person the whole thing, including the bit you're ashamed of, and letting them not fix it. Hard physical work helps too, a long swim or digging out a garden bed, something that uses the anger up.

You pick people on purpose, and once you've picked, you're in with the whole of yourself. What surprises your partners is how badly you want to be known and how hard you resist being worked out. You'd like them to understand you without having to explain, and if they get it wrong you go cool on them. Taurus is opposite Scorpio, and a lot of Scorpio Suns end up with someone who has a bit of Taurus in them, steady, physical, happy with an ordinary Tuesday night and the telly on. That person frustrates you by not wanting to talk about the relationship. They're also showing you that love can be easy some of the time and still go deep. When you want something from them, name it. Hinting and then watching to see if they notice is a test, and they'll usually fail it.

At work you need real say over your own patch. The title matters to you less than whether anyone is checking over your shoulder, and you'll put up with low pay for a long while before you'll put up with being micromanaged. You're good at the jobs other people avoid. Turnarounds, investigations, the audit, the patient nobody can get through to, the account that's about to walk. You like finding out what's really going on, and you're good at keeping it to yourself until the right moment. The Mars in you makes you competitive in a quiet way. You don't need to be seen winning, you need to have won. The trouble is loyalty in both directions. You'll stay years for a boss who backed you once, and never quite forgive one who didn't. Every so often check whether you're still in a job because it suits you or because leaving would feel like losing.

At twenty a Scorpio Sun is usually all or nothing about everything. You fall for people completely, you hold grudges completely, and you cut friends out with a thoroughness that frightens your mother a bit. You test the people you love to see if they'll stay. By the mid-thirties most have lived through at least one real ending, a divorce, a death, a career that collapsed, and come out the other side, and it changes them. The intensity is still there, but it's got better aim. You stop testing and start asking. The fifties often bring a kind of authority people don't argue with, and younger people bring you their worst news first. The thing to keep an eye on then is the old grudges, which a fixed sign can carry for decades without noticing the weight.

Pick one thing you've been keeping back from someone close to you. Nothing huge, just something ordinary you've been holding as an advantage, a worry about money, what you really thought of their friend, the job ad you looked at. Tell them this week, plainly, in one or two sentences, and then don't explain it or manage their reaction. Notice what your body does while you wait for them to answer.

asMoon.p: Your Moon is in Scorpio, and Death is Scorpio's card, so that's how this one reaches you. The Moon is in fall in Scorpio, which is the old term for a planet sitting in a sign that makes its job hard. The Moon's job is comfort, being soothed, feeling safe enough to let your guard down. Scorpio is fixed water ruled by Mars, and it doesn't trust easy comfort, so the Moon here has to go the long way round to get what it needs. Fixed means feelings don't pass through. They settle and stay. The Moon still gets fed, just indirectly, through closeness that's been tested, through privacy, through something being properly finished. On the card there's a small child in front of the horse, looking straight up at the rider without any fear at all. I'd say that child is nearer to how you feel inside than your face ever lets on.

Your feelings arrive quietly and then won't leave. Someone says something offhand at a family dinner and you're fine all evening, and at two in the morning you're lying awake replaying it word for word. A text from your ex's mum on your birthday can wreck a whole afternoon, and you won't mention it to anyone. When a friend cancels plans twice, you don't get cross. You make a small note somewhere inside and make slightly fewer plans with them afterwards. You need a lot of time alone with the door shut, and that's how you digest things, even if it looks like sulking to everyone else. Your moods sit in the body as well. Your stomach tightens before you know you're upset, and when something's wrong, sleep goes first and your appetite follows.

You remember the dates. When a friend's dad dies you're at the funeral like everyone else, but you're also the one who texts on his birthday the following year, and the year after that, when nobody else does. You know grief doesn't stop when the casseroles do. People tell you things they've never said out loud, because they can feel that you won't flinch and you won't pass it on, and they're right on both counts. A Scorpio Moon also has a very good ear for the gap between what someone says and how they feel. Your teenager says the party was fine and you know within a second it wasn't, and you know to wait until the car, where they don't have to look at you.

With the Moon in fall, comfort feels a bit suspicious to you. When someone's kind for no reason, part of you goes looking for the reason. You can be offered exactly the reassurance you wanted and not be able to take it in, because you've already decided it's just what people say. Jealousy lives near here too, and it's usually quiet. You won't make a scene about your partner's new colleague. You'll ask one extra question about her each week, casual as anything, and keep the answers. The other version is punishing yourself for needing anything at all. You'd sooner go without than ask and be let down, and then you're hurt that nobody noticed you went without. The people around you can't always tell what they did wrong, and often they didn't do anything.

Stress goes inward with a Scorpio Moon. Something awful happens, a diagnosis in the family, a betrayal, a redundancy, and your first move is to shut the door and go under with it. You don't ring anyone. You might clean the entire kitchen at midnight, or lie in the dark with your phone face down. People who love you get one-word answers. About a week later it comes up through the body, a jaw that aches, a stomach that won't settle, sleep that breaks at four every morning, or it comes out as one sharp remark to someone who didn't deserve it. What actually helps is water, literally. A long bath, a swim, a walk in the rain. And one person, the same one each time, who's allowed to sit in the room without asking you to talk.

What you need from a partner is to feel you've been let all the way in, and that they've let you in too. Half-closeness makes you anxious in a way you don't always recognise as anxiety. It comes out as checking, testing, going cold to see if they follow. Cancer and Pisces share Scorpio's element, and people with those signs strong in their charts often feel easy to you straight away, because they don't need a feeling explained before they'll believe it. Touch matters a great deal to you, and being held for a long while after a hard day settles you in a way no talking does. The thing to tell a partner early on is that when you go quiet you aren't always angry. Sometimes you're just full, and you need them to stay in the room.

Your feelings need somewhere private to go during the working day, and open-plan offices are hard on you. You do your best work with a door, or headphones, or a job with long stretches on your own. You're often drawn to work near the hard parts of life. Nursing, hospice, counselling, crisis lines, funeral work, anything where people are frightened or something has gone wrong and needs looking at properly. You're steady in those rooms. The cost is that you take it home, and a Scorpio Moon doesn't unload easily. If a colleague hurts you, you won't raise it, but you'll trust them a little less from then on and they'll never know why. It's worth having one person at work you can say 'that got to me' to.

In your twenties a Scorpio Moon tends to feel everything at full volume and show almost none of it. You fall hard, you get hurt, you keep a very private list of who let you down, and you might not cry in front of anyone for years. The thirties are usually when something breaks the seal. A loss or a breakup gets past the guard, and you find out you can fall apart in front of someone and survive it. After that you pick people more carefully and you're kinder to your own moods. By the fifties the Moon has done a lot of its long way round. Many Scorpio Moons become the person the family rings when someone's dying. The risk later on is that old hurts set into a quiet bitterness about one or two people, and it's worth dealing with those while everyone's still alive.

When a feeling has been sitting in you for more than a day, write its name on a scrap of paper, one word, like 'jealous' or 'left out', and put it in your pocket. Carry it until you've said it to one person, in that same one word if you like. It doesn't need explaining. Then tear the paper up and put it in the bin.

asRising.p: Your rising sign is the one that was coming up on the eastern horizon when you were born, and it sets the first house, which is the body and the way you walk into things. With Scorpio rising, Mars becomes the ruler of your whole chart, with Pluto as its modern co-ruler, and Death, Scorpio's card, is the card people meet first. Scorpio being fixed water, what they meet is still on top with a lot going on underneath. In whole-sign houses Taurus then falls on your seventh house of partners, Leo on your tenth of career, and Aquarius on your fourth of home. So you arrive guarded and watchful, and you tend to end up with solid, plain-spoken partners, a public life that wants to be seen, and a home with a lot of air and space in it. Look at the rider's face on the card. You can't read it, and strangers say roughly that about you.

You notice exits. Walk into a party and you've clocked where the door is, who's annoyed with whom and who's had too much to drink before you've got your coat off. In a job interview you give careful, short answers and watch their faces, and they tend to come away unsure whether you liked them. On a first date you ask most of the questions. People tell you you're hard to read and you're a bit pleased about it. Your body goes still when you're paying attention, which is most of the time, and strangers sometimes take the stillness as disapproval. You rarely start anything loudly. You wait, you get the measure of it, and then you move all at once, which is Mars running the chart, the long pause and then the strike.

Your instincts about people are usually right, and fast. You'll meet a new manager and know within one coffee whether they can be trusted, and it takes everyone else six months to catch up. That's the Mars ruler doing its job, scanning for threat, and it makes you good protection for the people you care about. Friends bring new partners round to meet you on purpose. The other gift, which nobody expects from someone who looks like you do, is a very dry sense of humour. You say one flat line at the worst moment of a bad meeting and the whole room breathes out. Because nobody saw it coming it lands twice as hard, and people remember you for it for years.

Being hard to read has a cost you don't always count. Because you never look flustered, people assume you're fine, and help doesn't get offered. Because you watch everything, you sometimes see a threat that isn't there, and treat a new colleague's friendliness as an angle before they've done a thing to earn it. You also hate being seen as a beginner. You'll skip the pottery class, or keep quiet in the language you're half learning, sooner than look clumsy in front of strangers. So a lot of good things never get started, simply because they'd have to be started in public. With Mars running the chart some of that is pride and some of it is defence, and you usually know which.

When things go wrong, Scorpio rising shuts the face down first. You get stiller, quieter and very polite, and you start sorting the people around you into safe and not safe. In a tense work meeting you say almost nothing, and afterwards everyone wonders what you're planning. After a breakup you might change your hair, delete the photos and turn up on Monday looking completely unbothered. A week or so later the body starts talking. Tight shoulders, a clenched jaw, a sudden need to be entirely alone for a weekend. The people close to you can feel the wall go up and don't know if it's there because of them. What helps, with Mars ruling the chart, is something physical and a bit fierce, a boxing class or a hard run, and then letting one person see your face with the composure off.

With Scorpio rising, Taurus sits on your seventh house, the house of partners, and it's very common for you to end up with someone steady, sensual, a bit stubborn and not remotely mysterious. They don't play games, and at first that almost bores you. Later it's the thing you trust most about them. Early on you're hard to get to know. You'll let someone talk for three dates and give them very little back, and a lot of good people give up before the fourth. Venus rules Taurus, so what your seventh house wants is pleasure without strategy, dinner that's just dinner. The lesson for you with a partner is showing interest before you're sure it's safe. Tell them you like them while it still feels like a risk.

Leo falls on your tenth house, career and reputation, which is an odd thing to have when your front door is Scorpio. You come across as private and watchful, and yet the working life that suits you puts you in front of people anyway, leading, presenting, being the name on the report. A lot of Scorpio risings get handed authority before they've asked for it, simply because they look like they can handle it. You interview well if the panel likes quiet competence and badly if they want sparkle. You're good wherever you need to read people fast, sales, negotiation, policing, journalism, HR during layoffs. What catches you out is recognition. The Leo tenth wants its credit and you're too guarded to ask for it, so say what you did, in the meeting, with your name attached.

At twenty Scorpio rising is mostly armour. Black clothes or the equivalent, a stare that keeps people back, a lot of watching at parties, and a real fear of being seen trying. People assume you're older and harder than you are. Through the thirties the face usually softens a little. You've been hurt, you've survived it, and you don't need the whole guard up for every stranger. This is often when the Leo tenth house starts to pay off, and people who used to find you intimidating start calling you impressive. By the fifties Scorpio rising tends to have real presence and far less need to defend it. You still see through people in about four seconds, and you're gentler about what you do with it. The risk later on is being so self-contained that nobody quite knows you, even at seventy.

At the next gathering where you hardly know anyone, choose one person and let them see you unsure of something within the first ten minutes. Ask what a word means, admit you've never been to this suburb before, say you're hopeless at these things. Keep it small and true. Then watch how they respond. Most people move a little closer, and that tells you something useful about how your face lands on strangers.

asBirthCard.p: This one doesn't come from any planet in your chart. It comes from your birthdate. Add up every digit, and if the total's over 22 add those digits together again, and a total of 13, 49 or 58 brings you to thirteen, which is Death. Thirteen is one more than twelve, and twelve is a complete set, twelve months, twelve signs, twelve houses. So thirteen is what comes after something has been completed. It sits straight after The Hanged Man, the card of hanging upside down and waiting, and just before Temperance, the card of mixing things back together slowly. Death is the moment in between, when the waiting stops and something actually goes. In the old Marseille decks the thirteenth card often had no name printed on it at all. In astrology the card belongs to Scorpio, but that's the card's own nature, and it says nothing about your signs.

As a lifelong pattern it shows up as a life that keeps changing shape, often on a schedule you didn't pick. You've probably moved house more than most. You look at photos from ten years ago and don't quite recognise the person, and it isn't only the haircut. There's a certain kind of conversation you seem to end up in a lot. A friend in a hospital corridor. A colleague telling you in the car park that their marriage is over. Someone at a wedding telling you about the brother who isn't there. You're also the one who clears out the house, whether it's your own after a breakup or a grandparent's after the funeral, and you're good at deciding what goes. The pattern asks very little of you in the quiet years. It's the turning points where it gets loud.

Timing is the gift people miss. You can often feel that something's finished a while before anyone else admits it, a project, a band, a friendship that's been running on memory, and you can say so without making it cruel. Groups need someone who can do that, and they rarely thank them for it. You're also good at the practical tenderness of endings. You know to bring food, to sit with someone without filling the silence, and to ring again three weeks later when everybody else has stopped ringing. At work you might be the one who winds down a team or a product properly, so the people in it land somewhere decent. It's unglamorous and it matters a great deal to the people it happens to.

The less obvious shadow is that you get used to endings and start expecting them. In a good stretch, a steady job, a kind partner, a year with nothing going wrong, you can feel oddly restless, or catch yourself waiting for the floor to give way. Some people with this card leave first so it can't be done to them. They quit the job just before the review, or end things once the relationship gets comfortable, and call it knowing when something's over. Sometimes it is. Sometimes ordinary happiness just feels unfamiliar and they don't trust it. Before you pull the plug on anything, ask whether it has actually died or only gone quiet for a while.

Under real pressure this pattern gets decisive very fast. A loss hits, or a job goes, and within days you're changing things, the flat, the hair, the phone number, the diet, as if you could get the next chapter started before the grief catches up. For a week or so that works. Then it stops working. The grief usually arrives late, set off by some small thing, a song in a shop, and you're undone in a way that surprises you. The people around you can find the speed of it hard to be near. They're still in shock and you've already packed a box. What helps is slowing the outside changes right down, no big decisions for a couple of months if you can manage it, and letting the sad part run at its own pace with someone there, even if all they do is make tea.

Across a lifetime your relationships tend to come in distinct eras, and each one changes you enough that you're a slightly different person going into the next. That's no failing. Some people with this card stay with one partner for fifty years, and the pattern shows up as that one relationship ending and starting again several times inside itself, after a move, after children, after an illness, after the kids leave home. Either way, the partners who suit you are the ones who don't panic when you change. The ones who want you exactly as you were on the day you met tend to find you hard work. If you're in something long, say so out loud when you feel one of those turns coming, so the two of you go through it together.

Your working life probably won't run in one straight line, and trying to force it into one tends to make you miserable. People with this card often have two or three careers, and the jumps between them look sudden from outside, though they've been coming for a long time. You're useful anywhere something needs closing, clearing or starting again. Restructures, estate work, turnarounds, palliative care, editing, demolition, the tail end of a project everyone else has lost interest in. Thirteen is also a card about what's left once the extra has gone, and you're good at cutting. The risk is cutting because you're bored, reorganising a team just because it's been stable for two years. Before you tear something down at work, check who else has to live in what's left.

In your twenties the pattern tends to feel like chaos. Things end that you didn't want to end, a first love, a first job, a family home, and you take each one as a disaster. By the mid-thirties most people with this card can see the shape of it. They've had two or three complete changes of life and they've noticed that each one left them more like themselves, even the ones that hurt badly. They get quicker at telling a real ending from a bad month. The fifties often bring the endings that come to everyone around then, parents, bodies, careers winding down, and thirteen people are usually unusually good at meeting those, because they've had the practice. The work later in life is letting some things stay, and finding out you can enjoy a long stretch where nothing changes much.

Once a season, go through one drawer, one folder on your computer or one list of contacts, and let go of three things that belong to a version of you that's finished. An old email address, a gym card, the notes from a course you're never going back to. Before you bin each one, say out loud what it was for. Keep it quick. Twenty minutes, then shut the drawer and go and make a cup of tea.
